source.title: fmxcoders: Factorized Masked Crosscoders for Cross-Layer Feature Discovery
source.authors: A. Demou; Panagiotis Koromilas; James Oldfield; Yannis Panagakis; M. Nicolaou

record.tranche_reason: Tests sparse dictionary feature recovery and cross-layer feature structure in four pretrained LLMs, extending the topic beyond the original toy-model setting.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own sparse-probing, latent-category, and cross-layer coherence results. It cites Toy Models of Superposition but does not reproduce or test that paper's toy networks. Reconstruction metrics alone are not included as rows because they do not measure the claim versions.
record.test_reason: A methods paper. It trains crosscoder variants (fmxcoders) on LLM activations and reports how its own method scores against standard crosscoders and per-layer SAEs on probing F1, reconstruction, functional coherence and LLM-judge semantic counts. It assumes sparse dictionary features exist and uses dictionaries as a tool. It never asks whether LLMs hold features in superposition or whether dictionary features are canonical units. Method-versus-method gains do not bear on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that standard crosscoders learn latents functionally driven by one or two layers despite evenly spread decoder norms, and that these latents collapse onto surface patterns. fmxcoders (tensor-factorized and layer-masked) raise probing F1 by 10–30 points over crosscoders, above the per-layer SAE. They also cut MSE by 25–50%, roughly double functional coherence, and yield 3–13× more semantic latents. Masking trades some F1 for coherence.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains sparse cross-layer dictionaries on activations from pretrained LLMs, with tensor-factorized encoder/decoder weights and stochastic layer masking; it does not use the original toy-network setup or its interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Functional coherence increases with masking probability; the paper reports a reconstruction/probing trade-off as masking increases. Factorization alone does not increase functional coherence. Ablations are on Pythia-410M, and the paper states that masking and rank settings appear model- and dataset-dependent.

fits_no_version.finding: Standard crosscoder latents have high norm coherence (>7 of 8) but functional coherence near 2. Their activation depends on one or two layers despite decoder weight spread evenly across layers. Factorization plus layer masking roughly doubles this to 3.8 (Pythia-410M).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-layer dictionary latents' apparent multi-layer support (decoder norms) overstates their functional cross-layer dependence. How cross-layer the latents are depends on the dictionary's architecture and regularization.

fits_no_version.finding: Which latents a dictionary recovers (semantic versus surface, and probing quality) changes strongly with architecture at matched parameter count and sparsity: 3–13× more judge-labelled semantic latents, and F1 shifts of 10–30 points.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dictionary-recovered features in LLMs are method-dependent rather than canonical. This is a possible V5-adjacent claim, but the study does not frame it as a test of canonicity.

record.problems: The study uses eight post-MLP residual-stream locations from middle layers rather than full network depth. Semantic/surface labeling relies on GPT-4o-mini, whose reliability the authors caution is imperfect. Main-table results use a single training run per LLM and variant. The reported uncertainty is limited; no uncertainty estimates are given for the main probing and judge-count tables.

untested.parts: No toy models; no sparsity transition or geometry.
No test of capacity competition as a cause of polysemanticity.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
Does not test whether LLM features are spread across neurons or recoverable by dictionaries. It assumes this and compares dictionary architectures.
No direct test of completeness, stability or canonicity, though the latents learned clearly depend on the dictionary architecture.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from tests/T3 to uses_without_test/T4. Every row compares the study's own dictionary method with baselines and does not test superposition or SAE feature recovery as a property of the LLMs. The record's V4 labels are dropped. Toy Models of Superposition is cited only as background.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-model superposition, feature overlap, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether neuron polysemanticity is caused by competition for limited capacity or important features receiving dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemanticity arises from causes other than capacity pressure.
The study tests recovery of sparse-dictionary features in LLMs, but does not directly measure feature distribution across many neurons.
Completeness, stability, and canonicality of SAE features.
Whether features are fundamentally one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional.
